Separating real disruption from shop floor noise
How long is the capacity gone?
Response options and finite capacity rescheduling
Information flow from machine to planner
Microsoft Fabric, Power BI and automation boundaries

takeaways: Only a confirmed loss of capacity, judged by expected loss, recovery window and exposed orders, should trigger re-planning, not every PLC signal.
Planners need a repair range with a confidence level, an impact list that explains dependencies, and a small set of response options tested with finite capacity.
Fabric and Power BI provide governed facts and visibility, while scheduling logic proposes options and people approve the changes that reach the shop floor.
hook: When a critical machine goes down, ERP may still show capacity that no longer exists while the shop floor improvises. This episode guides production planners, plant managers and IT/OT architects from disruption detection and impact tracing to finite-capacity rescheduling, so the factory gets a revised plan it can actually execute.
